svg.aria-label: Diagram: an AWS Organizations resource control policy is attached where the resource lives, while a service control policy is attached where the caller lives. AWS states that an SCP limits permissions of IAM principals within the organization's member accounts while an RCP restricts IAM principals external to those accounts making requests to resources within them. RCPs never grant permissions and the effective permissions are the logical intersection of RCPs, SCPs, identity-based and resource-based policies. The policy is one-directional: AWS's worked example shows that an RCP on Account A applies to its S3 bucket even when accessed by users from Account B outside the organization, but does not apply to resources in Account B when accessed by users in Account A. RCPs reach principals regardless of organization membership, including root users. They cover a subset of services, 62 on the documented list, which excludes EC2, Lambda, RDS, IAM, CloudFormation, ECS, EKS and SNS. Four things cannot be restricted: resources in the management account, service-linked roles including their trust policy, AWS managed KMS keys, and the kms:RetireGrant permission. The RCPFullAWSAccess managed policy is attached everywhere, cannot be detached, and lets requests pass through RCP evaluation without granting access.
svg.title: Attached where the resource lives, not where the caller lives
svg.text: An SCP guards the caller. An RCP guards the bucket.
AWS Organizations resource control policies — deny-only, resource-owner scoped, 62 services.
SCP — attached where the caller lives
“limit permissions of IAM principals
within your organization’s member accounts”
Answers: where may my principals send data?
see also VPC endpoint policies — #44
RCP — attached where the resource lives
“restrict IAM principals that are
external to your organization accounts”
Answers: who may reach my resources?
reaches root users · any organization · deny-only
The worked example that settles the model — it runs one way
A bucket in Account A, inside your org, with an RCP. A bucket policy grants Account B, outside your org.
B reaches A’s bucket → “That RCP applies … even when accessed by users from Account B”
A reaches B’s bucket → “that RCP does not apply to resources in Account B”
It protects your resources from anyone, and your data in their account from no one.
Coverage: “a subset of AWS services”
IN s3 · kms · sts · secretsmanager · sqs
dynamodb · ecr · logs · signin … 62 total
OUT ec2 · lambda · rds · iam · cloudformation
ecs · eks · sns
Driven by the “Resource type” column of the
Service Authorization Reference, not by importance.
Four things it cannot restrict
1 any action on management account resources
2 service-linked roles — and their trust policy
3 AWS managed keys for KMS
4 kms:RetireGrant
3 and 4 sit inside a service that IS on the list — so
“KMS is covered” does not mean what it sounds like.
The default is the absence of a Deny, not the presence of an Allow
RCPFullAWSAccess is attached to the root, every OU and every account, and “You cannot detach this policy”.
It lets requests “pass through RCP evaluation” — and “This AWS managed policy does not grant access”.
DENY WINS ANYWHERE root → OU → OU → account any one of them can deny the permission
“even if the resource owner attaches a resource-based policy that allows full access to any user”.
And the documented rollout points the opposite way from the sales pitch.
AWS “strongly recommends that you don’t attach RCPs to the root of your organization without thoroughly testing”
— begin with individual test accounts, move up to lower OUs, then work upward. Measure with CloudTrail
Access Denied errors.
Requires all features enabled. And an RCP never grants: a principal with no IAM policy still has no access.
